events.excerpt: One of the struggles with vintage computer systems is that many of the ICs in them have no modern-day version that you can just purchase and drop-in. Creating replacements that use modern-day ICs inside has consequently become a popular direction, with [Philip Smart]’s TranZPUter being one such example . Standing for ‘transformable ZPU Computer’, the tranZPUter is transformable in the sense that it features an FPGA or MCU and the initial iteration targeting the ZPU Evo CPU design. This has led to a number of variants of this concept, including a version targeting the Z80 , the 6502 and 6809. These are based around the RP2350B MCU, using its PIO peripheral to great effect. Of these the Motorola 6809 is probably the lesser known MPU, having been launched in 1978 as an 8-bit MPU with some 16-bit features that could beat the 6502 in many metrics courtesy of its more advanced hardware. It being more expensive led to it only being used in systems like the TRS-80 Color, Dragon 32/64, SuperPET and a whole range of arcade systems. If you have any of those 6809-based systems and the MPU gave up the ghost, you can drop in the Pico6809 board featuring said RP2350B MCU as well as an ESP32 co-processor. Currently it targets the Dragon 32/64 systems, adding not just a fresh MPU, but also adds v

events.excerpt: Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks. ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese. ) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation
events.headline: Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model

events.excerpt: Polymarket markets reacted quickly to news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation amid reporting about three affairs, two with employees and one with a Megaspeed exec who may or may not be a Chinese spy. Protos used the Polymarket API to attempt to better understand exactly how quickly these markets react to this type of news. Markets about Huang’s future reacted quickly to the reporting of the second affair and his possible ousting. Read more: How Alice Huang helped Nvidia with Chinese export restrictions Polymarket’s market predicting whether or not Huang would resign or be removed by December 31 reacted quickly to both the reporting of the second affair and to the report that the Nvidia board was considering removing him. Indeed, it seems that looking at the second-by-second data, the market started moving mere seconds after the New York Times piece was published and even quicker after the publication of the Wall Street Journal piece that suggested he may be ousted. The difference here may simply come down to precision in the timestamps; each only has a timestamp accurate to the minute, and both moved within two minutes. Rebuffo made the announcement on X on Friday, November 13, where he said that his new role is focused on “applied AI x Client Dev,” adding that he “will be working alongside the technical teams and the management.” The hire comes after a year in which at least eight senior researchers and leaders left the nonprofit. From high-school contributor to the Merge engineer Rebuffo is not a typical new hire. In an interview given in October 2025 , he recounted starting on TurboGeth, the project that became Erigon, while still in high school, and becoming one of Ethereum’s youngest core developers at 17. Rebuffo was the principal engineer on Erigon during the Merge, which was Ethereum’s switch in 2022 to proof-of-stake. He took over as the client’s CTO by age 22. His work at Erigon focused on prototyping features and squeezing more speed out of the protocol without changing it through hard forks. The skill he names as most important is adversarial thinking: assuming any code he writes will be attacked. His new role at the foundation focuses on AI. events.excerpt: How do you think you're going to die? If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident." In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Read full article Comments
events.headline: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away

events.excerpt: Kraken’s parent company, Payward, earned much less in the third quarter because fewer people traded crypto, according to the company’s financial results for the third quarter of 2026. The falling price of bitcoin is also hurting Payward’s loans. The company has not listed its shares on the stock market yet, and it is trying to prove it can earn through a down cycle. Why is Payward earning less? Kraken’s parent company, Payward, makes most of its money from fees when people buy and sell crypto. It also lends money to other crypto companies. However, falling crypto prices are hurting both parts of its business. With less people trading due to price drops, Payward is collecting fewer fees. The bitcoin that borrowers put up as security for their loans has also lost value, which makes those loans riskier. The company’s third-quarter numbers already show the drop in fees. According to a letter sent to shareholders, Payward’s adjusted EBITDA was $60 million, down 67% from a year earlier. The total value of trades on the platform fell 30% to $353 billion. Its platform margin, which it now reports instead of adjusted revenue, fell 12% to $487 million. However, the number of accounts holding any money rose by 37% to 7.1 million. The quarter was also better than the one before it. Adjusted
events.headline: Crypto downturn hits Kraken twice, as exchange and as lender

events.excerpt: The AI Compute Race report prices GPU compute outside the biggest buyers: a three-year commitment cuts the median price by 48%, while 17 of 22 tracked GPU models rose in price over the past year DALLAS, Texas – November 13, 2026 – Fluence has published The AI Compute Race , a report that prices GPU cloud compute for every company that is not a frontier lab or a hyperscaler. It was produced with research partners NEAR AI , io.net , Boundless , Phala , Gensyn , Fortytwo , Theta , Compute Labs and GAIB . Its central finding: where a company buys a GPU-hour sets the price. Across H100, H200 and B200 models, hyperscalers list GPUs at 1.98 times the GPU-cloud median, from 1.4 times on the B200 to 2.8 times on the H100. The same H200 lists from $4.08 to $10.60 an hour. Commitment length matters almost as much as provider choice. Against each provider’s own on-demand rate, a one-year reservation cuts the median price by 21% and a three-year term by 48%. Spot capacity lists at 53% of on-demand, for workloads that can be interrupted. Buyers who expect GPU prices to fall may need to recheck their budgets. events.excerpt: A South Korean court has jailed a money launderer for two and a half years in a fake-coin investment scam, using a new crypto protection law for fraud. Prosecutors are now using the Virtual Asset User Protection Act against ordinary scams, even without a referral from regulators. What did the court decide in the fake-coin scam case? A court in Goyang found that a ring ran a fake investment website and sold tokens that did not exist. The scammers told buyers the tokens were cheap and would pay off once they were listed on an exchange even though they never planned to give buyers anything. The man who laundered the money, known only as “A,” was sentenced to two and a half years in prison. “A” became a registered gift-certificate dealer, giving the scammers a bank account to receive the money in. From late December 2024 to February 2025, fourteen victims sent him about 501 million won (roughly $345,000) in 76 transfers. After he received the money, he would send it along to the “higher ups” as cash or vouchers, earning up to 150,000 to 200,000 won a day (roughly $103 to $138) for his efforts. The Goyang branch of the Uijeongbu District Court gave the sentence in July. “A” appealed, but the appeal was rejected in October, making the sentence final. “A” was convicted under Article 10,
events.headline: Goyang court convicts fake-coin launderer under Korea's crypto user law

events.excerpt: Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30. Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. S ome 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names. Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ , users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com , with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code.
